title: Reserved Top Level DNS Names
summary: Sets aside a few top-level domain names such as test, example, invalid and localhost for testing and documentation, and reserves example.com, example.net and example.org as second-level names. Using them avoids clashes with real websites.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 2606 sets aside specific domain names for testing and examples so that practice exercises do not accidentally interfere with real systems on the Internet.

subtitle: A set of top-level and example domain names kept aside so tests and examples never collide with real ones.

tldr.problem: When people invent top-level domain names for testing or documentation, those names can later be adopted for real use, which can cause confusion or make test code reach real systems.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 2606 reserves four top-level domain names (.test, .example, .invalid, .localhost) and three example second-level domain names (example.com, example.net, example.org) for use in testing and documentation only.
tldr.outcome: These names are reserved to prevent collisions with real domain names; RFC 2606 is a BCP that is updated by RFC 6761.

today: RFC 2606 is a Best Current Practice (BCP 32) that is updated by RFC 6761.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The Domain Name System (DNS) defines a tree of names rooted at ., with top-level domain names directly below it such as .com and .us. Below top-level domains are additional levels of names.

RFC 2606 notes that when organizations invent top-level domain names for local testing, those names can later come into global use. That can cause local test versions to conflict with real data, or test and example code to access real systems if run outside a restricted environment.
sections.plainLanguage: Names on the Internet follow a hierarchy. If people make up top-level names for testing, those made-up names could later become real ones and cause tests to affect real systems.

sections.title: Reserved Top-Level Domain Names
sections.content:
RFC 2606 reserves four top-level domain names for use in testing, documentation and examples:

  • .test for testing current or new DNS-related code.
  • .example for documentation or examples.
  • .invalid for constructing domain names that are clearly invalid.
  • .localhost traditionally defined to point to the loopback IP address, reserved for that use.
sections.plainLanguage: Four names are set aside for safe use in tests and examples: one for testing code, one for examples in documents, one for obviously wrong names, and one that always means 'this computer'.

sections.title: Reserved Example Domain Names
sections.content: In addition to the four top-level domain names, the IANA also reserves three second-level domain names for use as examples: example.com, example.net and example.org.
sections.plainLanguage: Three full example domain names are also set aside so that documents can show sample addresses safely.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: RFC 2606 states that using current or future top-level domain names for experimentation, testing, examples or invalid-name indicators can cause confusion and conflict. Test software can escape and run against the global operational DNS, and example names can become problematic if later used in practice. Reserving these specific names minimizes these risks.
sections.plainLanguage: Setting aside these specific names helps keep test activities separate from real systems and reduces the chance of accidental conflicts.
